title: Capacity-led routing savings playbook (wip)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working playbook for a capacity-led smart routing policy that prioritizes utilization of committed (reserved) capacity, then low-cost spot pools, and finally on-demand/burst. The goal is to produce a spreadsheet-driven cost model and a short set of heuristics that product and infra teams can use to tune routing for predictable unit economics while preserving latency SLOs.

Executive summary (quick):
- Problem: naive region/spot routing can leave reserved capacity underutilized and blow committed discounts.
- Idea: make routing capacity-aware: route to reserved pools first (respecting per-customer isolation), then to spot where latency budget allows, then to on-demand as last resort.
- Outcome: expected 6–22% cost reduction for mixed workloads (estimate band depends on spot fill and reserved utilization).
- Status: spreadsheet prototype + sensitivity scenarios included below; seeking infra validation and an SRE performance check.

Key assumptions used in the model:
- Reserved capacity pricing: effective GPU-hour $2.40 (amortized committed monthly price).
- Spot capacity pricing: average GPU-hour $0.55 (varies by region); availability volatility modeled as probability of preemption per 10 minutes.
- On-demand pricing: GPU-hour $3.10.
- Typical request profile: 70% short (<=128 tokens), 20% medium (129–1024), 10% long (>1024).
- Latency SLO: p95 <= 320ms for short/medium, <= 900ms for long (end-to-end).
- Batchability: short requests can be batched aggressively (avg effective tokens/request 60); long requests often unbatchable.
- Cache hit rate: prefix/KV cache reduces token compute by 12% on average.

Spreadsheet layout (recommended sheet tabs):
- Inputs: region prices, reserved commitments (hours per day), spot price distribution, latency headroom per route, token-cost-per-GPU-second mapping.
- Workload profile: request counts by size bucket, token distribution, batching windows, diurnal curves.
- Routing rules matrix: candidate pools (reserved-region-A, reserved-region-B, spot-pool-A, spot-pool-B, on-demand), eligibility flags, latency penalty estimates, preemption risk factor.
- Cost simulator: timestep-based simulation (1-min buckets) that consumes available capacity and computes cost & missed-SLO events.
- Sensitivity scenarios: slider inputs for spot availability (0.6–0.95), reserved utilization (0.5–0.95), SLO headroom (0–50ms).

Important spreadsheet columns (per-pool):
- pool_id, pool_type (reserved/spot/on-demand), region, committed_hours_remaining, baseline_price_per_gpu_hr, effective_price_per_token (calc), p95_latency_estimate_ms, preempt_risk_per_min, cold_start_penalty_ms

Routing policy recommendation (heuristics):
1) Reserved-first, soft-fill: route to matching reserved pool while keeping a small warm-buffer (5–10% of capacity) to absorb bursts without cold starts.
2) Spot-second, risk-aware: route non-latency-critical or batchable short/medium requests to spot when p95(headroom) >= estimated preemption penalty (preemption penalty modeled as 250–600ms depending on pool).
3) Regional affinity: prefer same-region reserved pools until their utilization > 85%, then expand regionally to respect networking latency budget.
4) Cost leak guardrail: if reserve utilization below 55% for 6+ hours, reduce expansion to spot/on-demand to force internal routing to reserved pools (trades latency for unit-cost savings).
5) Canary fallback: on high preemption (observed preemptions in last 15m > threshold), evict spot routing for in-flight canary traffic and move to on-demand/reserved.
6) Customer isolation: for customers with private/dedicated capacity, preserve routing to their pools unless explicit agreement to share capacity.

Example scenarios (spreadsheet output snippets in plain text):
- Scenario A (steady traffic, high reserved utilization): reserved utilization 92% -> cost reduction 18% vs naive on-demand routing; SLO compliance 99.6%.
- Scenario B (diurnal spike, low reserved utilization): reserved utilization 52% -> naive routing wasted reserved, cap-led policy forced more traffic into reserved (slight p95 increase +40ms) but saved 9% cost.
- Scenario C (spot instability): spot availability 0.62 and preemptions frequent -> policy automatically reduced spot share for p95-sensitive buckets; net savings 6% after preemption overhead.

Sensitivity observations (quick):
- Spot preemption cost is nonlinear: small increases in preemption probability drive up retry/cold-start costs rapidly. Model this with a 2-stage cost (immediate retry cost + additional latency penalty cost converted to SLA credit estimate).
- Committing to more reserved capacity gives diminishing returns when utilization < 65% — model should flag underutilized commitments and recommend rightsizing.
- Network egress differentials between regions can negate spot price savings for large-output workloads (embeddings/long generation). Add an egress cost column.

Open questions / data needed from infra & finance:
- Validate our amortized reserved GPU-hour values (finance to confirm actual effective blended monthly price after discounts).
- Real-world spot preemption distributions by region (SRE to provide recent 3-month histograms).
- Cold-start/caching empirical penalty numbers for our serving runtime at different pool sizes.
- Is cross-tenant bursting into reserved pools allowed legally / by product policy? (privacy/customer-isolation question).

Operational concerns and mitigations:
- Observability: add per-pool metrics (preemptions, fill-rate, avg-queue-time) into Redwood Console and wire to routing controller for real-time decisions.
- Fallback loop safety: implement exponential backoff when moving traffic between pools to avoid oscillation on marginal signals.
- Billing alignment: ensure cost attribution maps to customer accounts when routing uses shared reserved capacity.

Next steps (practical):
- Jonah: add region spot preemption histograms to the spreadsheet (due 2026-03-05).
- Priya: confirm reserved pricing amortization with finance and update model (due 2026-03-08).
- Markus: SRE to run a 3h failover test (spot -> on-demand) against a synthetic workload and capture cold-start penalties (due 2026-03-12).
- Product: validate recommended heuristics with two pilot customers (opt-in) and measure realized savings.

Appendix: short checklist for a pilot rollout
- Define pilot customers and their isolation constraints.
- Baseline run: collect 7 days of traffic and reserved utilization.
- Create simulation in spreadsheet and share results with customer.
- Run canary (10% traffic) for 24h with full telemetry.
- If safe, ramp to 50% for 48h, then full.

Notes to self (raw):
- Need a simple visualization: stack chart of cost by pool over time + SLO hit markers.
- Consider an automated recommender that marks 'reserved rightsizing' opportunities and creates a ticket.
- Think through product messaging: "Reserved-first routing" may be confusing; prefer "capacity-aware routing" in customer docs.

End of draft.

(Spreadsheet prototype: capacity-led-routing-sim-v1.xlsx attached in Drive in the same folder - TODO: export and link once cleaned.)
